issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette:
Marisol had crossed the border from Honduras years before, but the worst night in her life still felt as if it were happening in fragments she could not put away. During the flight north, the van in which she was being transported stopped for a checkpoint, and men in uniforms leaned in close, barking orders over the smell of alcohol on their breath. One of them grabbed her arm as he spoke, and the sharp, sour odor became fused in her mind with the sound of commands, the hard flash of authority, and the knowledge that there was nowhere to go. In the years since, those same cues had kept returning with the force of a warning: a whiff of alcohol in a hallway, a supervisor’s clipped instruction, a correctional officer’s uniform in the prison where she worked as a guard. When those cues appeared, Marisol immediately changed what she was doing — taking the longer route through the prison corridor, turning her face away, or keeping herself busy with paperwork — because she could not bear the surge of alarm they brought on. Each one made her body react before she could think, with a rush of danger that felt immediate and real, and she had come to believe the world was dangerous and people were not what they seemed. At times she looked at herself and could not recognize the woman who had become so watchful and so easily frightened. The more she saw herself that way, the more the border scene came back to her with painful clarity, as if she needed to keep finding the moment she had been changed.

Marisol’s life had narrowed around keeping herself from being caught off guard. She avoided being around people in authority or uniform whenever she could, and at work she chose her seat in the break room, the meeting room, even the cafeteria, based on where she would have the most protection at her back and the clearest view of the door. The way she organized her days only sharpened what she feared, because every avoided hallway, every guarded seat, and every uniform she tried not to notice kept the prison full of reminders that she was still living around the event. After shifts she turned on loud music or the television just to keep her mind from settling on what had happened. When she found herself dwelling on how the event could have been prevented, she would replay the border crossing over and over, imagining different choices, different routes, different moments where she might have escaped. Each time she resorted to those habits, she felt more certain that she could not cope without them, as if the very need to keep herself distracted proved how fragile she had become. Keeping herself that occupied meant the memory was never really put down anywhere, and when it did break through it came back with even more force, loud and intact. Those efforts gave her brief relief, but they also kept the event close and made the smell of alcohol, the sound of orders, and the sight of a uniform even more potent, because they returned her attention again and again to what she feared most. The more she arranged her life around avoiding those reminders, the more those same things seemed to stand out to her — a slurred voice in a hallway, a sergeant’s shirt, the stale smell of beer on an inmate’s breath — until ordinary shifts felt crowded with signals. The more she tried to keep away from those reminders, the more she felt her world shrinking and her confidence in other people eroding.

Sometimes the memory broke through with startling clarity. She could hear the men’s voices in her head exactly as they had sounded that night, and the scene would come back in such vivid detail that she had to stop whatever she was doing and breathe until the wave of emotion passed. After those intrusions, Marisol found herself thinking that if the memory could still take hold so completely, there must be something deeply wrong with her, and that she had never really left the woman who froze at the checkpoint. When that happened, she reacted as if danger were right in front of her: a sudden movement nearby in the prison corridor could make her flinch hard enough to embarrass herself, and she would scan every room for exits, certain that something bad was about to happen. That constant sense of danger made the memory harder to keep away, so on the worst days it would surface again without warning, pulled up by the very alarm she could not switch off. The memory and the threat feeling fed each other until she was left with the conviction that she was still in the same kind of danger. After those episodes she became even more convinced that the world could turn hostile without warning, and that she no longer knew herself well enough to trust her own judgment. Feeling that exposed all the time only confirmed, in her mind, that the world was not safe and that she was the kind of person who had to keep bracing for the worst. She would then throw herself back into distraction, turn the TV louder, avoid the officers in uniform at work, and keep choosing the safest seat she could find, but the relief never lasted long. Each time she did that, the prison around her seemed to fill with more and more triggers — every corridor, every set of boots, every sharp command becoming part of the map of what she was trying not to remember. Those habits also gave her fewer opportunities to see that most moments were ordinary, so her fear stayed alive, and the very things she did to steady herself became reminders that she was always bracing for impact.

Recently, the cycle has tightened at the prison. A supervisor’s order delivered across the corridor, the smell of alcohol on an inmate’s breath, or a uniformed sergeant stepping too quickly into her line of sight can set off the same surge of alarm and bring the memory rushing back. Marisol has started calling in sick more often and feels ashamed that she cannot explain to her husband why she is so jumpy and distant. What finally brought her to treatment was realizing that she was living as if every day might collapse into that night again, and that she was exhausted by the effort of staying on guard. She is hoping to feel like herself again, but what she fears most is that the fear will keep spreading until there is nowhere in her life left that feels safe. Each time she smelled alcohol or heard that sharp, ordered tone, her body read it as immediate danger, as if the checkpoint had opened again inside the prison. Those moments also pressed on her with a harsh thought she could not shake: that the world was dangerous, that people in power could turn on her without warning, and that she had been foolish to trust her own sense of safety.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes triggers leading to avoidance and distraction, but it does not clearly state the triggers themselves drive those maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette shows cues provoking alarm, but it does not explicitly state the triggers cause the perceived threat in the required causal way.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette includes negative beliefs, but it does not clearly state the triggers produce those appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette says negative appraisals are followed by memory replay, but it does not explicitly show the appraisals leading to the intrusive memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that negative appraisals lead Marisol to seek out or notice triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette links memory and negative beliefs, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes the negative appraisals in the required causal way.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows threat feelings accompanying memory, but it does not explicitly state the threat feeling drives the memory to intrude.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that perceived threat leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that perceived threat leads to triggering cues or their salience.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette describes maladaptive coping and then memory becoming more accessible, but it does not clearly state the strategies cause the memory intrusions.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies generate or worsen negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies lead to triggers or greater trigger exposure/activation.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
